deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of the 'Continuitätsbeweis' remark begun on the previous page). Claim: if f is single-valued (eindeutig) and continuous on [a,b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b) at least once. This is the intermediate value theorem.

Hilbert then shows that single-valuedness cannot be dropped. He uses a two-valued 'function':
- f(x) takes the value 1 for every x except x=a;
- f(x) takes the value 0 for every x except x=b.
So f(a)=0 only and f(b)=1 only. At every other x, f has both values {0,1}.

Read as a multivalued function, its graph is the union of the segments [a,b)×{0} and (a,b]×{1}. Each branch is locally constant away from the endpoints, so f is 'continuous' (two-valued) there. It still never takes a value strictly between 0 and 1. The remark presumably serves the continuity method of the previous page (uniformisation and covering surfaces): there one must make sure the map being continued is single-valued.

PART B (continuation of pp. 43 and 50: 'polar' function systems, i.e. orthogonality with respect to a weight that changes sign). Let X_n be the Legendre polynomials. Take α in (-1,1) not a zero of any X_n, and define
  P_n(x) = [X_n(α) X_{n+1}(x) - X_{n+1}(α) X_n(x)] / (x-α).
The numerator vanishes at x=α, so P_n is a polynomial of degree n.

[Mine] By the Christoffel–Darboux formula, P_n(x) = (1/(n+1)) Σ_{k=0}^n (2k+1) X_k(α) X_k(x). This is the Legendre kernel polynomial K_n(x,α). Its leading coefficient is proportional to X_n(α), which is why zeros of the X_n are excluded.

Claimed polarity property: ∫_{-1}^{1} (x-α) P_n P_m dx = 0 for n≠m and ±1 for n=m, after normalisation.

[Mine] Proof of orthogonality: for i<n, ∫(x-α) P_n x^i dx = ∫ [X_n(α) X_{n+1}(x) - X_{n+1}(α) X_n(x)] x^i dx = 0, by Legendre orthogonality since deg x^i < n.

The weight x-α is indefinite. So the 'norm' ∫(x-α) P_n² can have either sign, hence the values ±1. The next page shows it is nonzero: it equals -X_{n+1}(α) X_n(α)^2 · (h_n/k_n) · k_{n-1}…, nonzero when X_n(α), X_{n+1}(α) ≠ 0.

Completeness: P_0,…,P_n span the polynomials of degree ≤ n, so completeness follows from Weierstrass approximation.

Generation by a continued fraction. Put f(x) = ∫_{-1}^{1} (ξ-α)/(x-ξ) dξ = Σ_{k≥0} c_k / x^{k+1}, with moments c_k = ∫_{-1}^{1} ξ^k (ξ-α) dξ. Hilbert's marginal closed form is '(x-α) log((1-x)/(1+x))'.

Write P_n = A_0 x^n + A_1 x^{n-1} + … + A_n. Multiplying out, P_n f = (polynomial part) + Σ_j (1/x^j) {c_{j-1} A_n + c_j A_{n-1} + … + c_{j-1+n} A_0}. Hilbert writes the last term without the A_0 factor, i.e. A_0 = 1 tacitly.

The P_n are the denominators of the J-fraction (equivalently the Padé denominators at ∞) of f. This means the coefficients of 1/x,…,1/x^n vanish, so P_n f = Q_{n-1} + O(x^{-(n+1)}). These n linear conditions on the A's are exactly ∫ P_n ξ^i (ξ-α) dξ = 0 for i=0,…,n-1, which is the conclusion drawn on the next page.

Check against the next page (α=-1/2): the P's are proportional to 1, 3x-2, 5x²+8x-7. Hilbert indexes these from 1, whereas the formula above gives them as P_0, P_1, P_2.
errors: Part A: 'für alle Werte x ausser 0, 1 ist sie 2deutig' should read 'ausser a, b' (the exceptional arguments). 0 and 1 are the values, not the arguments, unless a=0, b=1 was tacitly intended.

The marginal closed form '(x-α) log((1-x)/(1+x))' is inaccurate. For x outside [-1,1], ∫_{-1}^{1}(ξ-α)/(x-ξ)dξ = -2 + (x-α) log((x+1)/(x-1)). Hilbert's version omits the constant -2 and has the opposite sign of the logarithm (up to iπ). This does not affect the moment argument, which uses only the c_k.
'= 0, ±1' holds only after normalising P_n by a constant. The unnormalised P_n as defined do not have norm ±1.
In the 1/x^j coefficients the factor A_0 multiplying c_n (resp. c_{2n-1}) is omitted, i.e. A_0 = 1 is tacitly assumed.
Minor indexing inconsistency: the formula with index n gives degree n (P_0 = 1), while the next page labels the first polynomials P_1 = 1, P_2 = 3x-2.

results.what: Intermediate value theorem requires single-valuedness; counterexample of a continuous two-valued function omitting intermediate values
results.modern_name: Intermediate value theorem; failure for multivalued (closed-graph) maps / need for single-valued branches in continuity method

results.what: P_n(x) = [X_n(α)X_{n+1}(x) - X_{n+1}(α)X_n(x)]/(x-α) are orthogonal polynomials for the sign-changing weight (x-α) on [-1,1]
results.modern_name: Christoffel's theorem / kernel polynomials (Christoffel–Darboux) for a polynomially modified weight; orthogonal polynomials for a quasi-definite (indefinite) moment functional
results.usually_credited_to: E. B. Christoffel (1858); Darboux (1878); quasi-definite theory: Chihara and others (20th c.)

results.what: Use of such systems as the simplest example of a 'polar' function system (orthogonality w.r.t. indefinite weight, norms ±1), linked to polar integral equations
results.modern_name: Polar (definitizable/indefinite) kernels; orthogonality in Krein-space-like setting
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1906, polar integral equations), Garbe, Marty; later Krein-space theory

results.what: P_n obtained as denominators of the continued fraction (Padé at infinity) of the Stieltjes transform ∫(ξ-α)/(x-ξ)dξ; coefficient matching gives moment orthogonality
results.modern_name: J-fraction / Padé approximants of Stieltjes transform; Chebyshev–Stieltjes continued fraction theory

deep.surprise_reason: Both items are standard. The intermediate value theorem remark is textbook, and the kernel-polynomial construction is Christoffel's 1858 theorem. It is nice to see it used as an explicit example of Hilbert's own 'polar' (indefinite-weight) orthogonal systems and tied to continued fractions, but this is a natural illustration, not a new result.
